title: Now let your servant go in peace
word: Now let your servant go in peace
tomorrow: if only three things remain, which one wins?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Te Deum: praise first, and a plea at the end. The line was we praise thee, O God. Today, a much shorter song, and a familiar one.
screen: `WE PRAISE THEE, O GOD.` → `A SHORTER SONG.`

segments.voice: Somebody hands you a newborn at a family party. The weight is wrong, lighter than you expected and heavier at the same time. The head smells like warm bread. Everyone goes a little quiet. In Luke's Gospel an old man named Simeon holds a baby in the Temple, and then says something that sounds alarming: now you can let me go. He isn't sick. He isn't sad. So why would holding a child make him ready to leave?
screen: `A NEWBORN IN YOUR ARMS.` → `NOW YOU CAN LET ME GO.` → `WHY WOULD HE BE READY?`

segments.voice: Listen to the whole sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; Because my eyes have seen thy salvation." There's the answer, in the word because. Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Messiah. Now his eyes have seen, and his arms are holding the promise. Some readers hear a watchman being relieved at the end of a long shift: the thing he was waiting up for has come, and he can rest. It isn't a wish to die. It's the peace of a promise kept. This is the Nunc Dimittis, and the path met it near the beginning, in Camp two. Catholics pray it at Night Prayer, the last prayer of the day, before sleep. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the Church ends its day with an old man's song about what his eyes have seen. Not a list of what's left undone. That's the senses of it: eyes that have seen, hands that have held. And that's why it sits here, near the summit. Five years on, the song asks a quiet question: what have your eyes seen along the way?
screen: `MY EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.` · `A WATCHMAN RELIEVED.` · `NOT A WISH TO DIE: A PROMISE KEPT.` · `THE LAST PRAYER OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Cup your hands in your lap as if they were holding something small and precious, and feel the weight you imagine there. Bring to mind one thing your eyes have seen on this road that you're glad of. Then slowly open your hands, palms up, and let them rest that way. If you pray, Simeon's words fit: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, in peace.
Now let your servant go in peace. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis: rest, because the promise has been seen.
screen: `NOW LET YOUR SERVANT GO IN PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this: in peace, not because everything's finished, but because something promised has been seen. Rest well tonight.

screen: `DAY 1789 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IF ONLY THREE THINGS REMAIN, WHICH ONE WINS?`

howItsDone: Catholics pray Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, every night at Night Prayer (Compline), and remember Simeon at the Presentation of the Lord on February 2.

fork.setup: your grandfather finishes building a backyard bench he promised you as a kid, sits on it, and says, "now i can rest." what's the Simeon reading?
options: he's tired and wants you to leave him alone.
a promise he carried is kept; that's his peace.
he's quietly telling you he's very ill.
fork.reveal: Simeon's peace comes from because: my eyes have seen. a kept promise lets a person rest, the way a watchman rests when the morning comes.

original.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the opening words of Simeon's song, prayed at Night Prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man saying he's ready to die.
what it means: the peace of seeing a promise kept, prayed by Catholics as the day closes.
what a scholar hears: Luke 2:29–32; the Greek apolyo, to release or dismiss, used of freeing a servant; the canticle in Compline.
guess: Simeon's song: rest, because the promise was seen
a priest's words sending people home after Mass
a prayer asking God for a peaceful death

chat.says: at my graduation Abuela said she can "go in peace" now. is she saying she's dying??
options: Probably not. It's Simeon's line: something she waited for came true. It's joy.
Yes. In the Bible those words always come right before someone dies.
It's just a polite way to say she's tired and ready to go home.
chat.meaning: Simeon says it because his eyes have seen what was promised. The peace is a promise kept, not a goodbye.

Simeon.meaning: a just, devout old man promised he would see the Messiah

Temple.meaning: the Temple in Jerusalem, the center of Jewish worship then

Nunc Dimittis.meaning: Simeon's song; Latin for now you dismiss

Night Prayer.meaning: the Church's last prayer of the day, also called Compline

Messiah.meaning: the anointed one God promised to send

Shape: senses (a newborn's weight, eyes that have seen). Practice kind: a body posture (cupped, then open hands).
